items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “The theory that behaviour is learned by observing and imitating others, especially role models”?
items.answer: Social learning theory
items.markingKey: Social learning theory: the theory that behaviour is learned by observing and imitating others, especially role models. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Bandura et al.’s study belongs to the learning approach. Reason (R): It investigated whether aggression could be acquired by observing a model. Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

items.stem: Explain how social learning theory differs from operant conditioning.
items.answer: Operant conditioning requires the learner to perform a behaviour and be reinforced; social learning theory says behaviour can be learned simply by observing a model, without direct reinforcement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark operant; 1 mark observational learning contrasted [2]

items.stem: Jonas, aged 5, starts copying wrestling moves on a younger cousin after watching wrestling on television with an older brother in Bogotá. Explain why the older brother may be a particularly strong role model.
items.answer: He is the same sex, familiar and of higher status, so Jonas identifies with him.
items.markingKey: 1 mark feature; 1 mark identification [2]

items.stem: Tomás, aged 5, starts copying wrestling moves on a younger cousin after watching wrestling on television with an older brother in Jakarta. (a) Use social learning theory to explain Tomás’s behaviour. (b) Suggest how Tomás’s parents could reduce the behaviour, using learning principles.
items.answer: (a) Tomás observed models (wrestlers, older brother) performing aggressive moves and imitated them; the wrestlers may have been seen as rewarded (cheered), which is vicarious reinforcement. (b) Model and praise gentle play, avoid watching violent programmes together, and do not reward the wrestling with attention.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark observation/imitation; 1 mark vicarious reinforcement or identification [2] (b) 1 mark modelling/rewards; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Explain why children might imitate a same-sex model more than an opposite-sex model.
items.answer: Children identify with models who are similar to them, and same-sex behaviour is more likely to be seen as appropriate and rewarded in their culture.

items.stem: Evaluate Bandura et al.’s (1961) study of the transmission of aggression, including a discussion of quantitative data.
items.answer: Strength (inter-rater reliability): Children’s aggression ratings were checked by two raters (r = 0.89), and the test-phase behaviour was observed through a one-way mirror by more than one observer, so the observations were reliable. Strength (quantitative data): Imitative aggressive acts were counted in 5-second intervals over 20 minutes, giving numerical data that allowed clear comparisons between conditions. Weakness (ethics): Children were exposed to aggressive models and were deliberately frustrated (mild aggression arousal), which may have caused distress and taught aggressive behaviour. Weakness (demand characteristics): A Bobo doll is designed to be hit, so children may have thought they were expected to hit it rather than imitating aggression. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Bandura et al.’s (1961) study of the transmission of aggression. Include at least one point about generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Children were matched on pre-existing aggression, and models followed a standardised script for ten minutes, so differences in imitation can be attributed to the model’s behaviour. Strength (inter-rater reliability): Children’s aggression ratings were checked by two raters (r = 0.89), and the test-phase behaviour was observed through a one-way mirror by more than one observer, so the observations were reliable. Weakness (generalisability): All 72 children came from one university nursery (Stanford) and were aged about 3–6, so the findings may not apply to other children. Weakness (ecological validity): Children watched an unfamiliar adult attack a Bobo doll in an unfamiliar room for a short time, which is unlike learning aggression from family or media in everyday life. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe the three stages of Bandura et al.’s procedure.
items.answer: Stage 1: each child played in a room while an adult model behaved aggressively or non-aggressively towards a Bobo doll (or there was no model). Stage 2: the child was taken to another room with attractive toys and mildly frustrated by being told they were for others. Stage 3: the child spent 20 minutes in a room with aggressive and non-aggressive toys, including a Bobo doll, observed through a one-way mirror.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Daniel counted imitative aggressive acts during 20 minutes of play for children who had seen either an aggressive or a non-aggressive adult model. Table: Imitative aggressive acts in 20 minutes — Aggressive model: 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 14. Non-aggressive model: 11, 7, 0, 5, 5, 4. What is the range of scores for the non-aggressive model condition?

Two observers watched the same 20-minute play session through a one-way mirror in a nursery in Lima and tallied children’s behaviours. Tallies — imitative verbal aggression: Observer 1 = 3, Observer 2 = 5; aggressive gun play: Observer 1 = 20, Observer 2 = 19; punching Bobo: Observer 1 = 14, Observer 2 = 17. Suggest one way in which the inter-rater reliability of this observation could be improved.
items.answer: Operationalise each behavioural category clearly with examples, and train the observers together on practice recordings before the study so that they interpret behaviours in the same way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: operationalised categories or training; 1 mark: explained [2]

items.stem: Chloe and a second observer independently recorded the behaviour of children in a playroom using the same categories. Tallies — imitative verbal aggression: Observer 1 = 14, Observer 2 = 14; non-aggressive play with tea set: Observer 1 = 11, Observer 2 = 8; mallet aggression: Observer 1 = 13, Observer 2 = 13; imitative physical aggression: Observer 1 = 8, Observer 2 = 8. (a) Explain how the researcher could check the inter-rater reliability of this observation. (b) Explain one weakness of a covert, controlled observation in this study.
items.answer: (a) Both observers record the same behaviour independently at the same time using the same categories; their tallies are then correlated, and a high positive correlation (for example above +0.8) shows good inter-rater reliability. (b) The playroom was an unfamiliar, artificial setting with specific toys, so behaviour may not reflect how children act at home or school.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: two observers record the same behaviour independently; 1 mark: scores compared/correlated with a high positive correlation [2] (b) 1 mark: weakness identified; 1 mark: explained in context [2]

items.stem: Discuss whether the ethical problems of Bandura et al.’s study outweigh its usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Children were exposed to violence and frustrated deliberately. Children could not consent. Arguments against: The findings informed debates about violence in media and the importance of role models. The aggression was directed at a toy and the procedure was short. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Kwame counted imitative aggressive acts during 20 minutes of play for children who had seen either an aggressive or a non-aggressive adult model. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) The standard deviation for the aggressive model condition was 9.40 and for the non-aggressive model condition was 1.85. Explain what these values show. (c) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study. (d) To what extent do these results support the prediction that children who observe an aggressive model will show more imitative aggressive acts than children who observe a non-aggressive model? Use the data in your answer. (e) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Aggressive model: 18.5; non-aggressive model: 1.5. (b) The aggressive model condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (c) Parental consent and a debrief, with the child playing with the non-aggressive model afterwards. (d) Mean for aggressive model = 18.5 and non-aggressive model = 1.5; the direction of the difference matches the prediction and the scores in the two conditions do not overlap and the sample is small (n = 8 per condition), so the results support it, although the small sample limits confidence; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (e) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that aggression is learned through observation? In your answer, you may refer to nature versus nurture and ecological validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: Children who saw an aggressive model imitated specific physical and verbal acts that controls rarely showed. Same-sex models were often imitated more, consistent with social learning theory. Arguments against: Boys were more physically aggressive than girls in all conditions, suggesting biological influences. Hitting a Bobo doll may be play rather than real aggression. The study measured immediate imitation, not long-term aggression. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Outline one strength and one weakness of Bandura et al.’s (1961) study of the transmission of aggression, with one point about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Children were matched on pre-existing aggression, and models followed a standardised script for ten minutes, so differences in imitation can be attributed to the model’s behaviour. Weakness (ecological validity): Children watched an unfamiliar adult attack a Bobo doll in an unfamiliar room for a short time, which is unlike learning aggression from family or media in everyday life.

items.stem: Evaluate Bandura et al.’s (1961) study of the transmission of aggression, including a discussion of ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (quantitative data): Imitative aggressive acts were counted in 5-second intervals over 20 minutes, giving numerical data that allowed clear comparisons between conditions. Strength (inter-rater reliability): Children’s aggression ratings were checked by two raters (r = 0.89), and the test-phase behaviour was observed through a one-way mirror by more than one observer, so the observations were reliable. Weakness (ethics): Children were exposed to aggressive models and were deliberately frustrated (mild aggression arousal), which may have caused distress and taught aggressive behaviour. Weakness (ecological validity): Children watched an unfamiliar adult attack a Bobo doll in an unfamiliar room for a short time, which is unlike learning aggression from family or media in everyday life. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: A researcher in Lisbon is interested in whether children copy helpful behaviour that they see on video. Plan a laboratory experiment to test this. Your plan must include: the type of data collected, the sampling technique, how the dependent variable will be measured and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: helpful or neutral video; DV: number of helpful acts in a play session. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Lisbon, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.
